new.text: Accounting rules let the loss stay hidden while the bank promised to hold the bonds to the end. A run forced a sale, and the paper loss became real in a day. The bonds were never in default. SVB's held-to-maturity losses were about $15.1B, close to all of its owners' money. Two days after SVB closed, the Fed opened the Bank Term Funding Program, which lent to banks against Treasuries at their face value, not their market value. A bond's price can fall, but in that panic its value as collateral was held at par by policy.

blocks.text: Why do governments sell tickets? Much of each year's new borrowing repays old tickets that are ending. The rest covers the gap when spending is more than taxes. For a government that issues its own money, borrowing is also a rule it sets for itself: in the US the Fed may not buy new Treasuries straight from the government (Level 1, "How money is born today"), and safe bonds help a central bank steer interest rates. Banks, pension funds and central banks also need a safe ticket to hold. Each new ticket is sold at an auction where dealers must bid. The resale price then works like a vote that never stops: if buyers doubt a government's plans, yields rise and its interest bill grows.

That bill is already large. Malaysia's debt service is projected at RM57.3 billion in 2026, 15.8% of revenue, above the 15% limit Malaysia set itself in its 2023 fiscal law (Act 850). In the US, net interest passed $1 trillion in fiscal 2026, more than defense.

new.text: The title passes, with one correction. Bonds are the backbone of the system's plumbing: collateral, reserves, liquidity and stablecoin backing. They are not what most bank deposits lean on. At US banks, loans are $14.1T of $25.9T of assets, Treasuries and agency bonds $4.8T. In normal years most new deposits are born from loans. In 2020 to 2021 most came from the Fed buying bonds and the government spending (Level 2, "Who really creates money"). Either way, the system settles, pledges and saves in Treasuries.

new.label: How to learn this chapter
new.text: Read each part once, then close the page and answer the stop-box questions from memory. In a classic study, students who tested themselves three times remembered 61% a week later, against 40% for students who reread four times (Roediger and Karpicke, 2006). Guess before you open each curiosity question, then check the answer. Come back in three days for the Day 3 card. 'Learning styles' have no good evidence behind them, and highlighting and rereading help little (Pashler and others, 2008. Dunlosky and others, 2013).

new.text: Two rules fall out of the seesaw. Yields up, prices down. And the longer the ticket, the bigger the swing. A point means one percentage point, say from 4% to 5%. For a one-point rise, a 2-year ticket falls about 2% and a 30-year ticket about 15% (a model). A bond's duration tells you its swing: a fund with a duration of 6 falls about 6% per one-point rise. Fund factsheets print it.

new.myth: Government bonds are safe, so you cannot lose money on them.
new.reality: They are safe from default, not from price. In 2022 the main US bond index lost 13.01%, its worst year since the index began in 1976. Hold a single bond to the end and you get every ringgit back. Sell a fund's units after a dip and the loss is real.

new.text: There are two markets. The first sale is the government's auction, a ticket booth. In Malaysia, Bank Negara runs it and 20 principal dealers must bid. Every later sale is at a resale stall, the secondary market: one investor sells to another through a dealer. The government gets nothing from resales, but the price shows what its next auction will cost.

The price shown is the clean price. The buyer also pays you the interest earned since the last payment.

new.label: Five starting questions

items.q: Why did the G20 move within months in 2008 to 2009, but take years on poor countries' debts?
items.a: Two games. 2009 was a stag hunt (box 1): the shared fear of collapse made each member expect the others to act, and out came a $1.1 trillion package. Debt relief is a free-rider game (box 2): relief from one lender frees cash to pay the others. The 2020 pause covered $12.9 billion, but only one private lender joined, and Ethiopia's deal took more than five years to reach agreement in principle.

items.q: If every country wants a tariff edge or a cheaper currency, what happens when they all try at once?
items.a: Tariffs are the clean prisoner's dilemma (box 3): all lose when all raise them, as in the tariff war of the early 1930s. Currencies are murkier: in the 1930s devaluing helped the countries that did it, and historians find that devaluing together would have sped recovery (Eichengreen and Sachs, 1985). Exits have been deals like the 1985 Plaza Accord, or truces like the October 2025 US and China pause, which can lapse. Two giants trading threats are playing chicken.

items.q: Why does the world keep saving in US dollars even while complaining about the US?
items.a: A focal point (box 4). Money is useful because others use it. The dollar was 56.7% of world reserves in mid 2026, nearly three times the euro. The yuan was 2.1%, largely because China keeps capital controls.

items.q: Why did Malaysia and its neighbours pile up dollars after 1998 instead of spending them?
items.a: To change the payoffs of a run on their currency (box 5). In 1997 to 1998 the ringgit fell from about 2.50 to about 4.88, and Thailand, Indonesia and Korea had to accept IMF conditions. Malaysia's reserves rose from $21.5 billion in 1997 to $132.6 billion in June 2026. Big reserves make attacking a losing bet, and mean the country need not accept the IMF's terms.

items.q: Why can Japan owe about twice its economy and borrow cheaply, while Sri Lanka defaulted?
items.a: A run on the debt (box 6): who holds it, and in which money, largely decides it. Japan owes yen mostly to itself: its central bank holds about 43% and foreigners about 13% (end 2025). Sri Lanka owed dollars to foreigners and stopped paying on 12 April 2022. Malaysia borrows in ringgit, but foreigners hold about a fifth of its bonds, so its risk is a weaker ringgit, not default.
